Gen X here. I grew up in an era of eye-rolling and pearl-clutching about how much we were overmedicating children. I have finally been diagnosed with ADHD and OCD after wasting years of my time and thousands of dollars on pharmaceutical and behavioral therapy for anxiety and depression that never really helped me “all the way.” 

The last psychiatrist I saw blew me off when I told her that I thought I had OCD. I concluded that my brain was broken in a way that couldn’t be fixed and gave up on ever feeling happy again. Then my young son was diagnosed with OCD and I went back and asked her to re-evaluate me. I finally got referred to a therapist specializing in OCD and feel hopeful for the first time in years. 

My therapist is the one who noticed that I also had ADHD symptoms. I initially scoffed at the idea—until she told me what the symptoms were. She said ADHD is underdiagnosed in girls and young women because they are able to mask it more effectively than boys, but that many women’s symptoms become acutely worse during menopause.

It’s appalling that I had to suffer major losses of function personally and professionally and ultimately  diagnose myself before I could get effective help from any of the mental health professionals I saw over the years. I don’t blame young women for taking matters into their own hands for a single second.

Increasingly, Chinese goods are routed through Canada (or Mexico), where Canadian firms perform limited assembly, and export finished goods to the U.S. under preferential terms.  The goods are improperly claimed as USMCA-eligible or Canadian-origin, circumventing the China-specific duty. 

The total value of transshipped goods -- including kitchen cabinets, trailer parts, many steel-related products -- may be as high as $303 billion a year, and growing.  Transshipment without “substantial transformation” is illegal under customs rules.

 Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, the illegal circumvention is semi-official Canadian policy.

The first cut is usually closes the pool forming a group that is "qualified" for the position. Then the second cut decides who to interview. The third step involves selecting from this now much smaller group who to recommend.

Some systems ask for a ranking of those recommended. Others don't. Ultimately the decision to make an offer is made by the Provost or President. But as a practical matter, most President's rely on their faculty to have conducted a rigorous process and follow their recommendation.

But despite this process subjective judgements enter the deliberations at every stage. And this is where things can go terribly wrong.

From this article it appears that Cambridge passed over two well qualified Black women to choose a candidate that would serve as a showpiece, a rags to riches cocktail party discussion accomplishment certifying the liberal character of the institution.

How or why did this happen? Because we do not have a reliable method of uncovering our own biasses during this process and putting them in check.

Tech executives with teenagers and young adults grapple with exactly the same issues around gaming, YouTube, and social media that every other parent does. I’ve worked with many families in this exact position — including prominent CEOs, tech execs and VCs — whose kids were spending hours every day/night on YouTube, gaming, TikTok and/or Instagram, and it took concentrated and intentional efforts to make long term behavioral changes.

Helping kids and teens make good decisions online and off is hard. comments.name: BigToeArthritis

In 1977, I was told, with intention to hurt, that my dad was not my biological father. In 2017, I learned through 23andMe that I had a half-sister. After carefully contacting her, I learned that I had a slew of half-brothers and sisters, nine in all, through my biological father. 

My biological father passed away from cancer in 1997, never knowing that I, and several other of his offspring, existed. It was neat to learn that he was 100% Italian, Sicilian to be exact. 23andMe even knew what city in Sicily the family roots could be found, Carlentini. I confirmed this through Ancestry.com and was amazed that 23andMe could figure that out from my genetics. 

My biological father gave me some great genes, I have a full head of hair at 67! When I saw his photo, I could see myself in him. I had a photo of him standing by his tent during the Korean War, and my own son thought the photo was of me!

But, I soon realized that shared genetics doesn't a family make. I never connected with my half-siblings beyond a superficial exchange of background info. It just wasn't meant to be - I no longer keep in touch with them. That's okay.

It's important, and really nice to know, that it often does work out and families are found and founded. I'm glad Ms. Moses shared this story.

The Canyon is a miracle of geology. Many early explorers assumed it was formed by some catastrophic event, partly because many believed that the earth was 6,000 years old. But we have long since learned that the canyon was carved out by the Colorado River over a million years or more.  And for me, the greatest attraction is all the layers of rock that reveal the course of erosion. So I climb from top to bottom and bottom to top to see it from every possible vantage point. Several times. Always wondering how that river did all that. 

Rafting along the river doesn’t appeal to me. But I understand if it appeals to you. I once loved to raft. But when I was at Denali, it struck me that the guide was very much in control, and I was just a paddle. And when I said that, a guide told me that the outfitter also had inflatable kayaks, where you have much, much more control than in a raft. I’ve never gone back. 

So my choice is to hike the Canyon rather than to raft it. And not to raft pretty much anywhere where inflatable kayaks are safe, like at Denali.

Although it may  help to compare our current corruption to just before the Roman Empire fell. Every day we soil ourselves on the world stage. Everyday!

comments.name: Carol Selsberg

articles.title: Inside Big Tech’s Frantic Race to Quell the Growing Backlash to AI
articles.summary: Tech companies are holding listening sessions, offering guaranteed jobs and writing big checks to win public support for the data centers they need.

comments.name: Peter C
comments.body: Another nail in the AI coffin.  It will rise from this coffin like a Frankenstein monster.

comments.name: TIMOTHY WOOD
comments.body: Our AI Overlords are bringing Adulthood's End. They must hate us. And our children.

comments.name: Theodore Crispino
comments.body: "Meanwhile, their top executives are increasingly talking about AI in ways that emphasize potential broad-based economic opportunity rather than job displacement or other scary scenarios. " In other words, don't listen to anything else we're saying. "Look at the shiny money! And pay no attention to the man behind the curtain!"

comments.name: Richard Gamer
comments.body:
This is good old fashioned democracy at work. Grass-roots efforts by local citizens have put big tech on notice that Americans are not pawns. And you can be pretty much guaranteed that the people involved in these efforts are neither entirely MAGA or DSA. 

If only we could work so cooperatively all the time. Because the truth is, there are messages to be read from both political extremes - big business and government are disenfranchising the average American. That's neither a fascist nor a communist message. It's a healthy reminder of who's supposed to be in charge here.

comments.name: John F
comments.body:
It probably would have been a good idea to not make the initial marketing push for this product "it's going to take all the good white-collar jobs and force you and your kids to work at Walmart for the rest of your lives".

I use AI on a daily basis in a professional and personal capacity but it's no surprise that people wouldn't be welcoming it with open arms.

comments.name: John Brack
comments.body: NIMBYism drove US industry out; tech could be next. To survive the backlash, tech firms must fund their own power, verify water recycling, and avoid exploiting taxpayers for stadium-style & other big business local & state subsidies—then aggressively advertise their self-reliance.

comments.name: will lowry
comments.body: zuck claiming his data center will be 200% water positive? can you explain how he plans on accomplishing that goal or do you simply 'believe' him?

comments.name: Annie
comments.body:
The great thing about the Valley is we're just a hop away from all the exciting features on the other side of "the hill" but when we're done there, we can go home to our quiet neighborhoods.
And Burbank airport is infinitely easier than LAX!

comments.name: lagreyeyes
comments.body:
I remember when the 213 area code stretched all the way through Westlake Village, where I grew up, to the Ventura County border. We definitely didn’t enjoy the sudden change to 818 and its association with the Valley.

Yes, just like those in “the city” (Los Angeles), we used to be condescending to the SFV. “Our beach!”, from original Malibu through Zuma, was our rallying teenage cry toward the provincial interlopers each summer. But after I moved out of my folks’ house into a Woodland Hills apartment, my attitude changed. So much to do! Movie theaters! Malls! So many restaurants on Ventura Blvd! Lots of fun and I really enjoyed the few years I lived there. Heckuva lot more exciting than WLV! Both the city proper and the SVF have their good and bad pockets, like all places.

(But never tell the now-snooty denizens of Calabasas that they’re actually part of the Valley. Everything over the Calabasas grade is. Yet they’ll ALWAYS deny it, lol.)

Long live the San Fernando Valley!

comments.name: GED
comments.body: Why would anybody want to live in the valley?  And this article certainly didn’t convince me otherwise. As for the “easier parking” claim, as an ex NYer parking in LA city is comparably a snap so….

comments.name: Matt
comments.body: Having grown up in the valley, I can confirm it is indeed the ugly stepchild. LA is a ugly city in general, but valley is so much worse, and miserably hot in the summer.

comments.name: Giveret Davar
comments.body: Not mentioned in the article or by any of my fellow Boomer Valley denizens was how lovely, peaceful & quiet the Valley was when we were growing up in the 50's & 60's.  Large swaths of the Valley were still farmland.  In the spring, the air was redolent with the perfume of the multitude of orange gloves, now sadly gone.  Some neighborhoods still boasted old farmhouses that gave the neighborhoods charm--much more charm than some of the mausoleum-type monstrosities seen now.  Things have advanced in many good ways since then, thanks to the civil rights movement, the women's movement, LGBT rights, etc.  But I sure miss those Orange groves whenever I come back to visit.

comments.name: Pardis
comments.body: Born and raised in the valley, never have I ever thought the valley is the “ugly stepchild,” or heard it spoken in that way. What kind of a title is this??? So insulting.

comments.name: Ma'at
comments.body: I spent most of my life in the 818, but only a few years within the la city limits. Most of my days were spent in Agoura Hills, at the very edge of the 818 and LA County, Raised 4 kids there, and my mom and dad and late wife are still there, buried on either edge of it. Long live the glorious 818!

comments.name: Nancy
comments.body: I grew up in Glendale, but spent a lot of time in Burbank and the north Hollywood area as a kid. Those were great memories of going to the movie theater in the. Mall and taking the bus when I didn't have a car. I have to say my childhood was pretty lovely. When I think about those times,  i feel really fortunate As a child, when you have enough resources in your community, live can treat you really well. We were blessed that my divorced single mother, could raise us in a safe neighborhood. We attended good schools that prepared us for university. Thank you for spotlighting this nexus of LA suburbia.

articles.title: The ‘Ugly Stepchild’ of L.A. Celebrates Itself on 818 Day
articles.summary: The Valley is often ignored in Los Angeles discussions, and residents once tried to secede from the city. But on one day each year, the region gets its recognition.

comments.name: Frostnow
comments.body: Really, lying across a dead log on a woodland trail near water?  There’s a tick bite waiting to happen.

comments.name: D
comments.body: I guess it depends on your definition of "friend".  Face Book ushered in a time where people now have hundreds, if not thousands, of "friends", most of whom they've never met or even spoken to.  Totally warped the concept of friendship and how to actually form one.

comments.name: J
comments.body: Many people don’t keep in all that close of touch with their college friends. I’m 34 and my experience has been that everyone has retreated into their busy lives of new parenthood and growing careers. I think this article discusses one aspect of a bigger picture; the flip side is that educated Americans are getting nearly all of their social interaction through their professional obligations. This is also depressing and distressing to those of us it is impacting. We are so overworked and overcommitted, we have no time or mental space left to simply be a good neighbor, do a favor for an acquaintance, or prioritize going to a church or community function. Let’s also stop being so afraid to admit that social cohesion functioned differently when most women did not work. They were the social engine of the family; now, as two-income households, we are barely holding it together to meet obligations for our closest friends and family and the social circle has shrunk. We can (and must) talk about this without jumping to the irrational conclusion that women should leave the workforce.

comments.name: c
comments.body:
This whole piece is based around the idea that people don't have agency.

"Graduating from high school meant the loss of an accessible infrastructure for connection, and with it a whittling down of peer groups, and no new structure — college, the military, a union, churches or civic groups — to take its place."

Then join a Church! Join the military! Go play pickup sports! Go volunteer!

We make so many excuses for people to ruin their own lives. Not all bad things people experience are done to them from the outside or "the system." There is no system! If you are in America you can do whatever you want. 

(Obviously there is an unlucky subset too consumed with, say, caring for sick family, or working too many hours to do things outside of work, but, again, that's not all these lonely people)

comments.name: James
comments.body:
A Friend is…
1. Is able to allow for two mutually exclusive ideas to exist.
2. Experientially knows the difference between sympathy and empathy.
👍

comments.name: Bob
comments.body: If people looking for friends read a third less of the deluge of articles about all the people looking for friends, they'd have time to make some friends.

comments.name: ROK
comments.body: My husband always has had work friends and he works in tech ops in aviation which is a pretty blue collar field. They are always doing something together be it helping each other with car repair, going out to lunch (and yes with an monthly trip to the gun range). He's also up to something with his hobby friends, be it sailing, fixing his car or flying model planes. His friends include doctors, engineers and guys who turn a wrench for a living. No one cares who went to college or what someone does for work. Maybe that's a Minnesota thing but I doubt it.

comments.name: sleeve
comments.body:
Why is this group, who is in the more socially favored gender, and are in the prime earning and social years of their lives, treated as such victims in this article?  Though it goes unmentioned, I would wager that most of those interviewed are likely of the most socially-favored race as well.  Maybe it is their lack of effort and initiative that is differentiating them?  They are not children or dependent in any way based on physical attributes, but we see them as having this great need for support?  If you won’t work and don’t leave your parents basement, I do not know what can be done to fix this issue because it is dependent on initiative and being willing to try.  It is easier to sit and complain how nothing is going your way than to get out there and meet people, but not very productive in alleviating their isolation.  People this age couldn’t wait for independence in prior generations.
Plus unmentioned is many of them are very connected via video games and chat groups, and even have mentors, but they are people like Rogan that keep telling them they are being dissed and mistreated, so his popularity soars since these guys have someone to blame….just like our prez.  Women are paid less for same jobs and brutalized much more by the very ones lamenting “oh woe is me”, and it gets a bit more than wearisome.

comments.name: Helena

comments.body: I saw them live in June 1975 at the Fairgrounds in West Fargo, ND.  It was brutally hot.  At one point Dusty Hill passed out on stage.  Billy Gibbons:  'Well, folks.  Dusty just bit the dust...'  Some dude came onstage and played bass the rest of the show.  Perhaps it was Elwood, I don't know.  RIP Frank Beard.

Greta can set sail with a Rag Tag group on a Fishing Trawler carrying bags of Doritos and canned Tuna to hand out on arrival and give a speech about Supremacy and the Right to Uncontrolled Migration - she should probably end it with a famous Roseanne Barr SPIT ON THE GROUND! comments.name: Matthew Zobian

comments.name: Laura
comments.body: What this article reveals, though not explicitly and perhaps not intentionally, is that this war is in part a civil war: the mother a medic in the Ukrainian army, one of her sons a soldier with the Russians. It reminds us that there was an 8-year Ukrainian-on-Ukrainian civil war before Russia ever invaded in 2022. The United States and Russia were both arming (different) Ukrainians in this civil war, so it was also soon a proxy war. 14,000 Ukrainians were already killed in it prior to Russia's 2022  invasion and cluster bombs were being used by the two sides to maim  one another. This begs the question "Which Ukrainians?" when we're asked to "support the Ukrainians."  Wouldn't a  compromise settlement and long term peace framework be the best possible way to "support the Ukrainians" at this point? Brother against brother and mother against son civil wars only become worse with no real "winners" morally or practically. Time to think outside the "box" of endless, fruitless war before this one also becomes a world war.

comments.name: DR

It is inspiring to read a story such a this, of perseverance and strength - may the war end soon, with Russia forced to give all Ukrainian lands back

The Ukrainians are the allies we should want, and every time I read again about this war, I am ashamed that we do not fight alongside them for freedom.

comments.name: Matsuda

comments.name: Aishwarya Mohan Gahrana
comments.body:
Private Education in India has not only become a debt trap but has also failed to provide an employable education. These education businesses focus on image-building rather than on building educational infrastructure. Even in primary education, private schools advertise Air Conditioners, swimming pools (not for swimming classes but for pool parties), car parking, etc. They have lavish halls for parents and teachers but an unequipped library and laboratory. 

In recent years, Indian students are getting more marks than earlier generations, but increasingly become unemployable!! 

Most private schools and universities are promoted or developed by political persons. Even if they are not politician at the beginning, parties value them for their influence over captive young voters in their educational captivity. These students are regularly asked to join their political masters' programs and vote for them.

Recently, I referred a law graduate from one of the universities named in this article to a decent law firm; she was rejected even before the interview started. This feeling is across courses.

Businesses say these "purchased" degrees are not of use to us. This is a sorry state of affairs for students, who are paying for education, not for a degree. 

We need an overhaul - from class 1 to the last. 

I am waiting for a follow-up story from the industry on why they mistrust students of these private institutes.

comments.name: Former Tea Party big player
comments.body: India's leaders have failed the people. Corrupt to the core. It is time  that its people change the leadership, thoroughly and hold them accountable. The majority young should prevail.  Anything else is a slow grind to mindlessness.

comments.name: Anonymous Human
comments.body: Fantastic news coverage as usual by the excellent Alex Travelli, and the NYT team in India. As someone who grew up in India in the 70s and 80s, I did well in the Indian education system till about high school, when I decided I had enough of memorizing enormous amounts of information for regurgitation on tests. I ended up moving into the US higher education system, where I could actually have a proper conversation with the professor, and we could debate things. Best of all, at work people cared that I solved real world problems, and if I solved a few, they gave me more. I tell people I failed in India, and succeeded in the US. If your focus is on practical problem-solving, you will do fine, with or without education, anywhere in the world. Education is about providing context, but you still have to have the tenacity and drive to help the world, and make a real impact, not just an impression. I feel for these students. However, the world is much different today than when I grew up. So many kids in India have a shot at being creative, and have so many different technology tools and business models at their disposal. They should not put themselves in a prison of their own making, whereby they think that education is going to be their ticket to the future. Education is good, but applying yourself is even better. Indian culture can trap people in thinking that education and status are what make a person. Self-discovery and self-definition are equally important.

comments.name: Deepak
comments.body: India is a preview of the challenges that will face Africa's youth in the coming decades as it's population surges and China's and Europe's dwindle.

comments.name: H.K
comments.body: One aspect not touched upon in the article is who exactly is setting up these private colleges, which largely lack basic infrastructure and are in many cases nothing more than a building with a board. It is mostly the politically connected, often members of parliament themselves, who've formed cartels and cornered the higher education market, using political connections to get new "universities" and institutes approved. The cost of education in these establishments doesn't reflect the quality of education imparted, but rather how much students are willing to pay to get a degree. With demand exceeding supply, no wonder they charge an arm and a leg, while barely making graduates employable. This is squandering the demographic dividend on a national, generational, scale.

comments.name: Jose
comments.body: Should we feel sorry for what is happening in India when workers in many other developing countries have dealt with the same harsh realities for decades? I notice a different attitude when I look for IT help on freelance platforms. Indian providers, experienced or novice are understandably trying to make money, but sympaty rarely enters the equation when they are selling those services. If you are lucky you get decent work; otherwise you end up paying an arm and a leg. AI now is disrupting that arrangemen too, especially for that army of Indian IT wannabes. Perhaps,the lesson is simple, globalization is much less attractive when the disrupting occurs at home.

comments.name: BC
comments.body:
Private colleges are becoming a scourge in post-secondary education.  Swap "India" for almost any country and the story is the same.

I wish governments would invest in public post-secondary institutions.  Clearly, there's an appetite for good education, which people are willing to pay for, which would help governments recoup costs and deliver revenues.  This would also lead to some uniforimity in education, leading to a better workforce.  Sadly, profit is trumping everything, starting by feeding on the fears of parents and students who are thoughtlessly funding this mess.  

If people and politicians would just take a breath and step back before acting.  Alas, critical thinking is missing on many syllabi these days.

comments.name: Jamal Icahn

I think India should make it illegal for any political parties to promise freebies. India is in dire need of manufacturing. India should spend heavily in manufacturing stuff. This will fulfill India's commitment of becoming self reliant, as well as will create a bunch of jobs.

comments.name: Perry J. Greenbaum
comments.body: Another military failure for the U.S., but it is not surprising. Here is sonething to think about. A large military budget does not equate to winning wars, neither does having all the latest weapons and bombs and warplanes. Wars are chiefly won by the strength and resolve of people defending their homes. This is what happened in Afghanistan and what is now happening in Iran.

comments.name: Frank Knarf
comments.body:
Reading Mr. Friedman's op-ed about changes to the"physics" of power relationships in warfare, I was bothered by something left out. It all depends on actual or percieved existential risk. The "big" powers do not lack the ability to anihilate the small powers. They are unwilling to employ the means becuase they do not see failure to "win" as an utterly catastrophic outcome. This somewhat fortunate circumstance will not always be present.

If, for example, Israel at some point concludes that Iran and it's proxies will soon have the means to accomplish what they say they intend and actually mean what they say, the forbearance we have seen may end. Deterence and religion do not mix well. And then we can ponder the extent of any restraining environments on the potential acts of thuggish strongmen in their decline, and I am not referring only to Putin.

comments.name: Alex K

comments.name: Seth

comments.name: RetiredDetective
comments.body: Economic pressure. Like currently on Russia or what has occured with North Korea for over 70 years. Don't forget Cuba. Plan Desperation is doom to fail just like Operation Furious Bluster. Now the question is, how much damage will this thoughtless campaign cost?

They knew this war was coming for decades, have learned to sustain themselves under sanctions, know they can handle the suffering and planned for all this.

comments.name: ksanger
comments.body:

They are all usually helpful, and they all sometimes have side effects.  Test them out at home before use on a vacation.
Motion sickness is related to the vestibular system, which is poorly understood.  The inner ear and eyes are involved, but undoubtedly there are complex pathways within the nervous system.  It is probably a multifactorial problem, and no single stimulus will always cause symptoms, nor will one treatment work for everyone.

comments.name: lambjams

Although the different types have different functions, like the H2 receptor is predominantly in the stomach, affecting digestion and stomach acid, there is some overlap and likely genetic variation. I have discovered that one antihistamine for allergies doesn't really work for my motion sickness. However, one targeting H2 receptors, which is supposed to be primarily stomach, affected my sinuses more than expected. I haven't had a chance to test it for motion sickness, but it's worth trying. One of the big causes was easy to spot: severe depression. The 2nd cause, much harder to identify, was discovered purely by accident. My mother had been having absent seizures right in front of us for months and none of us knew what we were seeing. I'm told that depression and other conditions can significantly increase the risk for absence seizures. But of course no one had told me in advance that they w were something we should be looking out for. Nor did they tell me that when she took antibiotics for a urinary tract infection the antibiotics would interfere with the anti-seizure medicine causing her to have what were called breakthrough seizures. We had to learn a lot of this information the hard way; and I can't help but believe that a lot of people that get locked away in memory wards don't actually have dementia but instead have some other issue that's been misdiagnosed as dementia. And, sadly, when a patient is in their 80s or 90s it's far too common for doctors just to assume dementia rather than looking any deeper.

comments.body:
Crete without the history and museums seems sad to me. And a waste of money. Like going to the Met  - but just for the coffee shop.

There are scads of places with sandy beaches, good food and more nightclubs than you could get around in a lifetime and are much cheaper and easier to get to from the USA than Crete. Crete is special because it has so much more than those places. But each to their own.

Give the Peloponnese a try next time. All the islands are overrun with foreign tourists (like me!) in the summer so that, even in Crete, it is hard to easily get a sense of 'being' somewhere different. Most places seem like Queens with better weather. But the Peloponnese is where the Greeks go on vacation. Stay in the old Venetian port city and ancient capital of Nafplion and explore from there, or just sit in Syntagma Square, drink a frappe, nibble some mezes and watch the Greek world go by.

The first trip was in late April-early May, and we loved Chania. It was not overcrowded; the weather was fine; and the harbor and fort were captivating. We also spent time in Agios Nikolaus and Elounda (their having been the site of a Walt Disney film starring Hayley Mills that sparked my adolescent fascination with the country), briefly visited Santorini and Paros, and several other places. We revisited Crete on our second trip the following year, as well as the Pelopponese and of course Athens. Best experiences of my life. I would go back to Crete in a heartbeat--the generous people (and cats), the food, the landscapes, the history and beaches. Unforgettable.

comments.name: smith
comments.body: Premier Zhu was the architecture of China's current economic model, an export-oriented model that depresses domestic consumption.  Under Zhu, numerous China's state owned enterprises (SOE) went bankrupt or otherwise reorganized.  Millions of SOE employees suddenly lost their jobs, and many families struggled. He is the person who took back the tax revenue from local government, so that the central government had the resources to invest in areas it prioritized, leading to China's dominance and eventual overcapacities in key industries.  Let's not cancel this part of the history.  President Xi essentially follows the same economic model Premier Zhu established.  The main difference is that China has since moved up the manufactural and technological value chain. The industries it focuses on are no longer the ones we want to source, but the advanced ones that we die to keep and dominate.  What's happening in China's economy is a natural evolution of what Premier Zhu had envisioned and implemented.  His model makes clearcut the effect of government policies on winners and losers.  Our politicians tend to refrain from dramatic policy changes.  But we end up with same number of losers of economic changes.  It's just our losers don't really know who to blame.

comments.body: Mr. Zhu was considered a reformer at the time and indeed was a force in pushing China toward capitalism. In 1997, I went with GM CEO Jack Smith to China to try to complete a deal that would result in Buick being the first American auto manufacturer in the country. That became the crown plant in GM’s system, the Shanghai auto plant. Interestingly, when we got on the plane for Beijing, we did not have a deal but we had faith that Mr. Zhu would help us get it over the line. At the same time, Vice President Al Gore was also in China trying to get us, Boeing and a few other big American companies access to the market but was shadowed by Chinagate, a foreign fundraising allegation. For days, we ran around in circles but nothing happened until the men at the top said so — and then everything happened. Al Gore and Li Peng toasted the deals in the Great Hall of the People’s and Jack Smith gave a global press conference with about 100 journalists in attendance.

Shiloh is incredibly small by comparison and hemmed in by the river at Pittsburg Landing. Both needed very different strategies, and Grant's genius and doggedness (combined with Confederate failures to seize the moment) in improvising were apparent at both places. A great general and a great man.

While it may seem like splitting hairs, those seeking to buy in the area may opt to focus on well-managed, well maintained smaller buildings with healthy financials and robust reserves that are only two habitable stories and therefore exempt from the new regs. With parking at a premium and king tide (among other climate) threat potential, an ideal option may be a three story building with parking at the ground level. comments.name: Steven Mintz
comments.body:
Florida’s post-Surfside condo crisis should be a warning to New York.
Many condo and co-op buildings have kept monthly charges artificially low by underfunding reserves and postponing major repairs. New York may face an even larger problem because much of its housing stock is older. Roofs, façades, elevators, boilers, plumbing, electrical systems, structural repairs, insurance, and energy requirements are imposing costs at once.
Low monthly charges can create a false sense of affordability. A building with inadequate reserves is simply shifting today’s expenses onto tomorrow’s owners who will face crushing special assessments.
The problem extends beyond private housing. New York’s public housing system offers a glaring example of what happens when maintenance and capital replacement are deferred. Residents live with deteriorating conditions because essential repairs were deferred year after year, allowing manageable maintenance needs to become enormous capital liabilities.
New York should require long-term reserve studies for co-ops and condos, fuller disclosure of expected capital needs, and realistic funding plans, while providing targeted assistance to cash-poor homeowners.
The lesson is simple: deferred maintenance eventually comes due. Whether in a luxury condominium or a public housing project, someone has to pay.

State-sponsored propaganda can easily project a myth of overwhelming military and economic might on carefully edited channels. However, real-world stress tests consistently expose those illusions. 

We saw a stark preview of this reality during Operation Sindoor, when Pakistan—relying heavily on Chinese military equipment—found itself metaphorically attempting to cross a turbulent river on a mud horse, only to watch the river dissolve beneath it.

In a 21st-century world where information moves faster than state censorship, reality will always break through the propaganda. 

China’s leaders may try to shape the narrative at home, but global digital transparency will ultimately reveal the true limits of their system.

But Arday's narrative - the one that helped secure such an exalted position - contained Bunyanesque whoppers and obvious falsehoods, such as being in the series Seven Up. Mute until age 11. The marathons, so easily disproven. The book that never was, the academic appointments that never were. It appears the ivory tower is so insulating that some who dwell there can no longer discern truth from lies - the very opposite of what a university is supposed to represent. Lies that were obvious to a non-academic like myself living halfway across the world. I hope this troubling and tragic story shines a fiery light on those responsible for projecting their fantasies onto this damaged human being.
